items.q: How does the Java Memory Model (JMM) work: happens-before, volatile, and visibility?
items.a:
**JMM** defines when one thread is guaranteed to *see* another thread's memory writes. The [[g:happens-before]] relation is transitive: if A happens-before B, every write from A is visible to B. **volatile:** - guarantees [[g:visibility]] — a read always gets the latest value, never a stale cache/register copy - blocks reordering around the variable - [[r:does NOT guarantee atomicity]] for compound operations (e.g. `count++` still races) **Common happens-before edges:** - unlock → lock on the same monitor - volatile write → volatile read - `Thread.start()` → code inside the thread - code → `join()` **Missing a single `volatile`:** 
class Worker {
    private boolean stop = false;      // missing volatile
    private int data = 0;
    
    void start() {
        new Thread(() -> {
            while (!stop) { }             // may run forever: JIT hoists stop out of the loop
            System.out.println(data);      // and may print 0
        }).start();
    }
    
    void shutdown() {
        data = 42;
        stop = true;                      // if stop is volatile, this write also publishes data
    }
}
Declaring `stop` as `volatile` fixes both bugs at once: the loop can exit ([[g:visibility]]), and `data = 42` sits *before* the volatile write so it becomes visible too ([[g:ordering]]). :::tip Takeaway visibility and atomicity are two separate problems. volatile handles visibility; if you need atomicity, use `AtomicXxx`/CAS or a lock. ::: :::deep At the [[o:hardware]] level: each core has its own store buffer/cache, and the CPU/compiler is allowed to *reorder* instructions for optimization. `volatile` inserts a [[g:memory barrier]]: - store-store + store-load around the write - load-load around the read These barriers are what create the happens-before edge — not "writing straight to RAM" as the popular explanation goes. **final fields** have special semantics: - once the constructor completes correctly, a final field's value is safely published to other threads without synchronization (the basis for safe immutable objects) - keep [[b:atomicity]] (CAS/lock), [[b:visibility]] (volatile/barrier), and [[b:ordering]] (happens-before) clearly separated — [[r:conflating the three is a common mistake]] - What handles `atomicity`: lock-free counters and stacks built with CAS, plus the ABA problem (23-java-concurrency-coding.async-the-modern-toolkit.q3). :::

items.q: Heap vs stack, escape analysis, and TLAB — why do they matter for performance?
items.a:
- [[b:Stack]]: one stack per thread, holding frames (local variables, references).
- [[b:Heap]]: shared objects, managed by the GC.

**Escape analysis** (JIT): if an object never escapes its method/thread, the JVM can:
- [[g:stack-allocate]] it (scalar replacement)
- or drop its lock ([[g:lock elision]])

→ reduces GC pressure.

**TLAB** (Thread-Local Allocation Buffer): each thread gets its own private allocation buffer inside Eden for fast, [[g:contention-free]] allocation.

:::tip Takeaway
most objects "die young" (the weak generational hypothesis) — that's why the GC splits generations and allocation in Eden is extremely cheap.
:::

:::deep
Escape analysis [[r:'fails']] (can't stack-allocate) when an object:
- gets stored into another object's field
- gets returned to the caller
- is passed into a method that isn't inlined

→ it then still goes to the heap. Enable `-XX:+PrintEscapeAnalysis`/`-XX:+EliminateAllocations` to check.

Allocating in Eden is a *bump-the-pointer* operation (just moves a pointer), so it's nearly free; TLAB lets each thread bump its own pointer without CAS.

**Real-world consequence:** hot loops that create garbage objects (autoboxed `Integer`, iterators, lambda captures) push the allocation rate up → more frequent minor GCs.
- measure allocation rate (MB/s) in the GC log
- reduce it by reusing buffers, using primitives, and avoiding boxing on the hot path
:::

items.q: Comparing GCs: Serial, Parallel, G1, ZGC, Shenandoah — when do you pick which?
items.a:
Choose a GC based on your [[o:SLO]]: throughput or tail latency.
GCCharacteristicPauseGood for
Paralleloptimizes throughputlongbatch jobs
G1 (default)region-based, predictable pausesmediummost services
ZGCfully concurrent, colored pointers< 1ms (TB-scale heap)p99.9-sensitive services
Shenandoahlow-pause concurrent (Generational since Java 25)< 1mslow-latency
Rule of thumb: throughput → [[g:Parallel/G1]]; tail latency → [[g:ZGC/Shenandoah]] (trading away some throughput/CPU). :::deep Be able to describe the mechanism, not just the name: **G1** splits the heap into ~2048 regions, prioritizing collection of the region with "the most garbage first" to hit its pause target (`-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis`). - pain point: [[r:humongous objects]] (> ½ region) and mixed GC **ZGC / Shenandoah** use *colored pointers* plus load/store barriers to relocate objects concurrently with the app → pause times stay nearly constant regardless of heap size (TB-scale). - trade-off: CPU cost for barriers + somewhat lower throughput **Choosing by SLO:** - p99.9-sensitive API (seat-hold, payment) → ZGC - overnight batch reconciliation → Parallel Always cite numbers when explaining: "switched G1→ZGC, p99.9 went from 320ms (GC pause) down to ~15ms." :::

items.q: GC tuning: heap generations, minor vs major/full GC, and signs of a memory leak?
items.a: **Generational heap:** Young (Eden + 2 Survivor spaces) and Old. - [[g:Minor GC]] cleans Young — fast, frequent - objects that live long enough get *promoted* to Old - [[o:Major/Full GC]] cleans Old — expensive, long pauses **Signs of a [[r:memory leak]]:** - repeated Full GCs where Old gen doesn't shrink - heap climbs steadily until OOM Common causes: a static collection holding references forever, a `ThreadLocal` never removed, unbounded listeners/caches, a ClassLoader leak (redeploy). Tools: heap dump + MAT, GC logs, `jcmd`. :::warn Fintech trap an unbounded cache is the most common source of OOM in high-traffic services — always set a max size + eviction policy. ::: :::deep **Leak investigation workflow:** - enable `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` + GC logging - open the heap dump in Eclipse MAT → check the *dominator tree* + "Leak Suspects" - trace the GC root holding the reference **Four classic culprits:** - unbounded cache (no max size/eviction) - `ThreadLocal` not `remove()`d in a thread pool (object lives as long as the thread does) - listener/callback never unregistered - ClassLoader leak on hot redeploy (Metaspace bloats) Distinguish a [[r:leak]] (Old gen climbs steadily, doesn't drop after a Full GC) from [[o:under-provisioning]] (frequent GC but reclamation still works). Citing "allocation rate" + "promotion rate" is a strong signal. :::

items.q: What are JIT compilation, the interpreter, C1/C2, tiered compilation, and warmup?
items.a:
The JVM starts by *interpreting* bytecode, while also counting how "hot" each method is.

Hot methods get compiled to machine code by the JIT:
- [[b:C1]]: fast compile, light optimization
- [[b:C2]]: slower compile, deep optimization (inlining, escape analysis, loop unrolling)
- [[g:Tiered compilation]] combines both

**Warmup:** peak performance is only reached once the JIT has compiled and profiled.
- benchmarks must discount the early phase (use JMH)
- also why GraalVM Native Image (AOT) starts fast but usually has lower peak throughput than a JIT that's fully warmed up

:::deep
Tiered compilation has 5 levels: 0 interpreter → 1/2/3 are C1 (different profiling levels) → 4 is C2.

Two mechanisms rarely mentioned:
- [[o:OSR]] (On-Stack Replacement): compiling mid-flight while a long-running loop is already executing
- [[o:deoptimization]]: when a speculative assumption (type profiling, a never-taken branch) is invalidated → falls back to the interpreter then recompiles (uncommon trap)

[[r:A full code cache]] (`-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize`) makes the JIT stop compiling → silent performance degradation.

A *megamorphic* call site (many receiver types) can't be inlined → slower. Use `-XX:+PrintCompilation` to inspect; benchmarks must always warm up (JMH).
:::

items.q: Traditional thread pools vs Virtual Threads (Project Loom) — what's the core difference?
items.a: OS threads are expensive (~1MB stack, costly context switches) → forcing bounded pools + async just to avoid running out of threads. [[g:Virtual threads]] (finalized in Java 21): threads managed by the JVM, mapped M:N onto a handful of carrier threads. - on blocking I/O → the JVM *unmounts* the VT from its carrier so the carrier can run something else Result: you write simple blocking code (thread-per-request) that still scales to millions of concurrent I/O tasks — without complex reactive code. :::warn Pinning blocking inside `synchronized` or a native call [[r:pins]] the VT to its carrier, losing all the benefit. Prefer `ReentrantLock` over `synchronized` on hot paths that use VTs. ::: :::deep **Mechanism:** VTs run on [[g:carrier threads]] (a ForkJoinPool, default ~#cores). When they hit blocking I/O that's already "Loom-ified" (sockets, NIO files, `Thread.sleep`, `java.util.concurrent` locks) → the runtime saves the continuation, unmounts the VT from its carrier → few OS threads still serve millions of requests. **Pinning** happens when a VT blocks inside `synchronized` / a native-JNI call: the carrier stays held, can't be unmounted. - detect it: `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full` - fix: switch to `ReentrantLock` **Note:** VTs solve *I/O concurrency*; they [[r:do NOT]] speed up CPU-bound work (still limited by core count) and don't remove the need to bound downstream load (you still need a semaphore/connection pool so you don't overwhelm the DB). - What it looks like to rewrite an existing concurrency exercise using virtual threads, including a real pinning trap (23-java-concurrency-coding.async-the-modern-toolkit.q4). :::

items.q: What do structured concurrency and ScopedValue (Java 21/25) solve compared to ThreadLocal?
items.a:
[[g:Structured concurrency]] (`StructuredTaskScope`): a task's subtasks form a block with a clear lifecycle.
- if one subtask fails/is cancelled, the rest are cancelled too
- avoids thread leaks and errors scattered everywhere

[[g:ScopedValue]] (finalized in Java 25): replaces `ThreadLocal` for passing context (request id, principal).
- immutable, clearly scoped (bound within a block)
- safer and cheaper when you have millions of virtual threads
- avoids the classic [[r:'forgot to remove a ThreadLocal']] leak

:::tip Takeaway
StructuredTaskScope manages a task's *lifecycle*; ScopedValue carries *context data* — together they replace the old ThreadLocal + hand-rolled ExecutorService pattern.
:::

:::deep
**API:**
- `ShutdownOnFailure`: one subtask fails → cancel the rest ("all-or-nothing")
- `ShutdownOnSuccess`: take the fastest result, cancel the rest (great for fanning out to multiple GDS/replicas to get the cheapest price)
- `fork()` starts a subtask on a VT, `join()` waits for the whole block → no leaked thread the way a self-managed ExecutorService can leak if you forget to shut it down

[[g:ScopedValue]] is immutable, only settable via `where(...).run()` (bound within a scope), and inherits safely into subtasks — unlike `ThreadLocal`, which can be `set()` anywhere and leak inside a thread pool.

- Placing `StructuredTaskScope` next to `CountDownLatch`/`CyclicBarrier`/`Semaphore`/`Phaser` to see what it replaces (23-java-concurrency-coding.async-the-modern-toolkit.q2), and how to write it on virtual threads (23-java-concurrency-coding.async-the-modern-toolkit.q4).
:::

items.q: How does ConcurrentHashMap work? Why is it faster than Hashtable/synchronizedMap?
items.a:
Instead of locking the whole map, CHM locks at the [[g:bucket/bin]] level: - CAS when a bin is empty - locks the bin's first node on collision - reads are nearly [[g:lock-free]] Java 8+ converts long bins from a linked list to a red-black tree (O(log n)) past a threshold. **Result:** multiple threads writing to different bins don't block each other → much higher throughput than Hashtable's single global lock. Note: `size()` is only an estimate; compound operations need `compute()`/`merge()` to stay atomic. **Compound operations are where mistakes usually happen:** 
ConcurrentHashMap<String, List<Seat>> holds = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
// WRONG: both operations are individually atomic, but the combination isn't
if (!holds.containsKey(id)) {           // T1 and T2 both see false
    holds.put(id, new ArrayList<>());  // T2 overwrites T1's list → the held seat is lost
}
holds.get(id).add(seat);
    
// RIGHT: a single call — CHM holds the bin lock while the function runs
holds.computeIfAbsent(id, k -> Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>()))
     .add(seat);
:::deep - init is [[b:lazy]]; resize happens via *transfer* one bin at a time, with multiple threads helping resize concurrently (each thread claims a range of bins via `transferIndex`) - size counting uses `baseCount` + a `CounterCell` array, LongAdder-style, to reduce contention → `size()` is only approximate - treeify triggers when a bin has ≥ 8 elements *and* the table has ≥ 64 buckets (below 64, it resizes instead of treeifying) [[r:A common race]]: a compound "check-then-put" must use `computeIfAbsent`/`merge` to stay atomic — an easy mistake when using CHM as a cache. - This exact "check-then-act" trap is the classic thread-safety question in LLD rounds (22-low-level-design-ood.patterns-in-interview-code.q3). :::

items.q: synchronized vs ReentrantLock vs StampedLock — when do you pick which?
How do you compose an async pipeline with CompletableFuture, and how is it different from Future?
items.a:
`Future` only has `get()` (blocking).

`CompletableFuture` lets you compose non-blocking pipelines:
- `thenApply`/`thenCompose` (chaining)
- `thenCombine` (merging two stages)
- `allOf`/`anyOf`
- `exceptionally`/`handle` (error handling)

You can specify an executor to control which thread runs it. With Java 21+, many cases are simplified with virtual threads + blocking code instead.

:::deep
[[r:Production trap]]: the non-Async variant of `thenApply` runs on whichever thread completed the *previous* stage — if that's an I/O/Netty thread, you accidentally block it → use `thenApplyAsync(fn, executor)` with an explicit executor.

The default `ForkJoinPool.commonPool` is shared JVM-wide → one slow task starves the whole app, and its size is #cores-1 (poor fit for I/O).

- [[r:swallowed exceptions]]: you need an `exceptionally`/`handle` at the end of the chain, or errors silently "disappear"
- Java 9+ adds `orTimeout`/`completeOnTimeout`
- `cancel()` does NOT interrupt a task that's already running

With Java 21, many CF pipelines can be replaced with virtual threads + blocking code for easier reading/debugging.
:::

items.q: The equals()/hashCode() contract — what happens if you violate it?
items.a:
[[g:Contract]]: equal per `equals` ⇒ same `hashCode` (the reverse isn't required). [[r:Violating it]]: two "equal" objects land in different buckets in a HashMap/HashSet → wrong lookups, silent duplicates. `equals` must be: reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent. Use the same set of fields for both; for JPA entities, prefer a [[o:business key]] over the id (the id is null before persisting). **Violating the contract loses elements from a `HashSet`:** 
class Booking {
    Long id;                                  // null until persisted
    public boolean equals(Object o) { /* compares by id */ }
    public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(id); }
}
    
Set<Booking> set = new HashSet<>();
Booking b = new Booking();
set.add(b);          // hashCode computed while id = null → bucket X
em.persist(b);       // DB assigns id = 1001 → hashCode changes → should now belong to bucket Y
set.contains(b);     // false — the object is still in the set, just in the wrong bucket
set.remove(b);       // removes nothing at all, the element stays stuck forever
:::deep **A classic JPA/Hibernate bug** — using a DB-generated `id` in equals/hashCode: - before persisting, id=null → every entity is "equal" - after persisting, id changes → the object already in a `HashSet` ends up in the wrong bucket, lost from the set **Fix:** - use an immutable *business/natural key* - or assign a UUID at the application layer before persisting - or use a constant hashCode (poor distribution but correct) [[r:Be careful]] with Lombok's `@EqualsAndHashCode`, which by default pulls in every field (including lazy associations → triggers a query/LazyInitException). Rule: base equals/hashCode on an *immutable* set of fields that identify the business entity, using `Objects.equals/hash`. :::

items.q: Immutability and the String pool — why does String's immutability matter?
items.a:
String's immutability gives us:
- [[g:thread safety]]
- stable map keys
- enables a *string pool* (interning) that reuses literals → saves memory

Immutability in general reduces concurrency bugs and makes code easier to reason about. It's a core principle behind value objects in DDD.

:::deep
- literals are interned at compile time into the string pool (which has lived in the heap since Java 7)
- `new String("x")` creates a new object; `.intern()` puts it back into the pool ([[r:be careful]] interning large amounts of runtime strings — it holds references and bloats the pool)
- Java 9's "Compact Strings" stores a Latin-1 `byte[]` instead of `char[]` → half the memory for ASCII strings
- concatenating in a loop should use `StringBuilder` (each `+` creates a new object)

The basis for DDD *value objects* (Money, Currency) — records are the modern way to create an immutable carrier; remember to defensive-copy any mutable-type fields.

Trivia: the string pool is a fixed-size hash table (`-XX:StringTableSize`) → interning too many runtime strings causes collisions & bloat. G1 has `-XX:+UseStringDeduplication` to merge `char[]`/`byte[]` arrays with identical content.
:::

items.q: Checked vs unchecked exceptions — the modern backend philosophy for error handling?
ClassLoaders and the delegation mechanism — when do they cause problems?
items.a:
ClassLoaders load classes using [[g:parent-first delegation]] (Bootstrap → Platform → Application).

**Real-world problems:**
- [[r:ClassLoader leaks]] on redeploy (a web app holds a static reference to an old class → Metaspace bloats)
- version conflicts between libraries

Understanding this helps you debug `NoClassDefFoundError`, `LinkageError`, and dependency hell.

:::deep
*parent-first delegation* is safe (prevents spoofing core classes), but SPI/JDBC/JNDI need the [[o:thread-context classloader]] to load implementations from a child classloader (reversing the delegation direction).

**[[r:Metaspace leaks on hot-redeploy]]** — an old web app instance is kept alive via:
- a static field
- a thread that never stopped
- a `ThreadLocal` holding a class
- a JDBC driver still registered with the old classloader

→ the whole ClassLoader can't be GC'd → Metaspace bloats until it OOMs on "Metaspace".

Tools: `-verbose:class`, heap dumps. Multiple versions of the same library → `LinkageError`/`NoSuchMethodError`, inspect with `mvn dependency:tree`. In K8s this is avoided entirely with immutable containers + restarts instead of hot-redeploy.
:::

items.q: What is off-heap / direct memory used for?
items.a:
`ByteBuffer.allocateDirect` allocates outside the GC heap.
- used for [[g:high-performance I/O]] (Netty, mmap)
- avoids copies, reduces GC pressure

In exchange:
- you must manage its lifecycle manually ([[r:easy to leak]] without releasing it)
- harder to debug

Many databases/brokers (Kafka) rely on the OS page cache + zero-copy following this same principle.

:::deep
**Mechanism:** a `DirectByteBuffer` allocates outside the heap, released *indirectly* via a Cleaner/PhantomReference when the GC collects the Java wrapper object.
- if the object lives long / the GC doesn't run → native memory never gets returned → a [[r:'leak']] even though the heap has plenty of room
- bounded by `-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize`

**Applications:**
- Netty's pooled allocator (avoids GC + copying)
- Kafka: OS page cache + *zero-copy* `sendfile` (no copy through user space), mmap for the index/log
- the Foreign Function & Memory API (finalized in Java 22) — the modern, safer replacement for `sun.misc.Unsafe`

Go deeper: off-heap trades "manual lifecycle management" for "reduced GC pressure" — worth it for latency-critical systems.
:::

items.q: How does HashMap work? Hashing, buckets, collisions, treeify, resize?
items.a:
HashMap = an array of buckets + a hash function. **The put(k, v) flow:** - compute `hash(key)` → pick a bucket (`index = hash & (n-1)`) - bucket empty → place the node there - [[o:collision]] (same bucket) → append to a linked list; if the key `equals`, overwrite instead **Treeify:** when a bucket has ≥ 8 elements *and* the table has ≥ 64 buckets → converts the list to a [[g:red-black tree]] (O(log n) instead of O(n)). **Resize:** when size exceeds capacity × [[b:load factor]] (default 0.75) → capacity doubles and everything is rehashed. **What a single `put` walks through:** 
static int spread(int h) {
    return h ^ (h >>> 16);        // mixes high bits into low bits, reducing collisions
}
    
map.put("VN8H2K", booking);
// 1. h = spread(key.hashCode()); i = (n - 1) & h   → n = 16, so i falls in 0..15
// 2. bucket i empty      → place a new Node there, size++
// 3. bucket i has a key  → compare hash then equals: if it matches, overwrite the value, size unchanged
// 4. different key       → append to the end of the list; if the list is ≥ 8 AND the table ≥ 64, treeify
// 5. size > 16 * 0.75    → resize doubles capacity; each node moves to i or i + 16, no full rehash
:::warn Trap a broken `hashCode`/`equals` "loses" a key inside the map (see 1.11). Using a [[r:mutable]] key and changing a field after inserting it means you can no longer find it. ::: :::deep Why capacity is a power of 2: it lets `hash & (n-1)` replace modulo (faster). HashMap also *spreads* the hash (`h ^ (h >>> 16)`) to mix high bits into low bits, reducing collisions. - [[r:not thread-safe]] → concurrent puts can lose data (Java 7 even had an infinite loop during resize); use `ConcurrentHashMap` instead (01-java-core-jvm.concurrency.q3). - allows one `null` key (bucket 0); `Hashtable` doesn't. - iteration order is [[r:not guaranteed]] → use `LinkedHashMap` for insertion order, `TreeMap` for sorted order. :::

items.q: ArrayList vs LinkedList — how do they differ and when do you choose which?
items.a:
ArrayListLinkedList
Structuredynamic arraydoubly-linked list
get(i)O(1)O(n)
add at endO(1) amortizedO(1)
add/remove in the middleO(n) — shifts the arrayO(1)* if already at the node
Memorycompact (just the array)costly (2 pointers/node)
**In practice:** almost always use [[g:ArrayList]]. - good cache locality (contiguous array), fast index access - LinkedList only wins when adding/removing a lot at [[o:both ends]] — and even then `ArrayDeque` should be used instead :::tip Takeaway LinkedList's O(1)* assumes you're already at the right node; getting there still costs O(n). That's why LinkedList rarely wins in practice. ::: :::deep `ArrayList.add` is amortized O(1): when full it grows ~1.5× (`newCap = old + (old >> 1)`) and copies into a new array → occasionally O(n) but O(1) on average. If you know the size in advance, use `new ArrayList<>(capacity)` to avoid resizing. - removing from the middle requires `System.arraycopy` to shift the tail → O(n). - neither is [[r:thread-safe]] → use `CopyOnWriteArrayList` (read-heavy) or `Collections.synchronizedList`. - iterating while removing → use `Iterator.remove()`, otherwise you get [[r:ConcurrentModificationException]] (fail-fast). :::

items.q: How do HashSet / LinkedHashSet / TreeSet differ?
items.a:
All three store [[g:no duplicate]] elements; they differ in ordering and cost: - [[b:HashSet]]: no order, O(1) add/contains — backed by HashMap - [[b:LinkedHashSet]]: preserves insertion order, O(1) — backed by LinkedHashMap - [[b:TreeSet]]: sorted by Comparator/natural order, O(log n) — backed by a red-black tree (TreeMap) **Choosing:** - just need fast dedup → HashSet - need stable insertion order → LinkedHashSet - need sorted order / range queries (`headSet`, `subSet`) → TreeSet
HashSetLinkedHashSetTreeSet
Iteration ordernot guaranteedinsertion ordersorted
add / containsO(1)O(1)O(log n)
Memory per elementlowestplus 2 pointersplus 3 pointers and a color bit
Allows nullone nullone nullno
Requires of elementsequals + hashCodeequals + hashCodeComparable/Comparator
Range queriesnonoheadSet, tailSet, subSet
:::deep HashSet is just a HashMap with a dummy value → every property (hashing, collisions, load factor) matches HashMap's. - TreeSet [[r:doesn't allow `null`]] (elements must be comparable); HashSet allows one `null`. - broken `equals`/`hashCode` causes HashSet to hold "silent duplicates" (two equal objects in two buckets) — same root cause as item 1.11. - `TreeSet` dedupes using `compareTo`, [[r:not]] `equals` — if two objects aren't `equals()` but `compareTo` returns 0, TreeSet silently drops one of them. A Comparator inconsistent with equals is a silent bug. :::

items.q: Cheat sheet: which collection for which situation?
items.a:
NeedUseBecause
Index-accessed listArrayListget is O(1), cache-friendly
Queue / Stack / DequeArrayDequefaster than the old LinkedList/Stack
Fast key→value lookupHashMapO(1)
Map that keeps insertion orderLinkedHashMap+ can double as an LRU cache
Sorted map/setTreeMap / TreeSetO(log n), range queries
Concurrent mapConcurrentHashMapbin-level locking (01-java-core-jvm.concurrency.q3)
**Rule of thumb:** default to [[g:ArrayList]] + [[g:HashMap]]; only switch when you have a measurable reason (ordering, sorting, concurrency). :::deep A few points senior interviewers like to ask: - [[o:LinkedHashMap]] with `accessOrder=true` + overriding `removeEldestEntry` gives you a few-line [[g:LRU cache]]. - `Arrays.asList()` returns a [[r:fixed-size]] list (add/remove throw `UnsupportedOperationException`). - a plain `array` (`T[]`) is the fastest and most compact but fixed-size and not generic-friendly → only use it on hot paths/primitives (`int[]` avoids boxing). - pre-sizing a large HashMap/ArrayList's initial capacity avoids repeated rehashing/resizing. :::
